note:
v1, EXTREME AND MEAN: THE SEVENTH SONG, A SKELETON (Harry, 17 Nov about 03:40: "open up 2 new song slots"). The record's slow song: 80, where the other six run 100 to 138.
The riff is two cells, a long (three sixteenths) and a short (two), and one rule: every long becomes a long and a short, every short becomes a long. Apply it again and again and you get a pattern of longs and shorts that never falls into a loop, yet every stretch of it comes back, and it is the same at every size. So the band plays the one pattern at many sizes at once: the guitars' muted strokes are the smallest cells; where a cell of eight or five sixteenths begins the string is let ring; where one of thirteen or eight begins there is a chord; where one of thirty-four or twenty-one begins, a crash; and the song's own eight sections go long, short, long, long, short, long, short, long: the long ones heavy, the short ones quiet. The form is the riff, 78 times slower. The kit keeps common time against all of it and starts its count again with each section.
In the quiet sections a wire harp (new on this record) has no written notes: the engine is given the same rule and plays it, each short cell a step higher than the long one that made it. In the last section the harp plays over the band.
The title is Euclid's phrase for a line cut so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer is to the shorter. Such a cut has no common measure; neither has this riff.
WHERE THINGS ARE: heavy 0:00, quiet 0:44, heavy 1:11, heavy on A flat with four guitars 1:54, quiet 2:38, heavy 3:05, quiet 3:49, heavy with the harp 4:16, one chord 4:59.

v2, THE SAME TUNE AT EVERY SIZE (a whole-song round, taken openly: the draw was Odd Sympathy, which I passed; v1's note said the three quiet sections were the same nine bars three times).
The song's idea is one pattern at every size, and the band already plays it so in the heavy sections. Now the harps do too. The first quiet section is as it was: one harp, the tune on the smallest cells (three and two sixteenths). In the second there are two harps: the new one plays THE SAME TUNE on the next size of cell (five and three sixteenths), an octave lower. In the third there are three: the third plays it on cells of eight and five, an octave lower again. It is a canon in which nobody starts late: the voices start together and go at different speeds, and the speeds stand to each other as the long cell to the short. Because the larger cells are made of the smaller, every note of a slower harp falls exactly with a note of the faster ones.
The engine plays all of it from the one rule; no harp has a written note.

v3, BREATH FOR THE LARGEST SIZE (a palette round, as drawn: the part the song lacked, on a sound no other song has).
The band plays the one pattern at many sizes, but one size had no voice of its own: cells of 21 and 13 sixteenths, about four seconds and two and a half. That is as long as a note can usefully be held, so it is where a tune can be sung slowly. In the three four-guitar sections (1:54, 3:05, 4:16) a brass section, horns and trombones, now plays the harp's tune on those cells, one long note to a cell. Strings are plucked for the small sizes; breath holds the large one. It is the same tune again (the canon of v2 went down three sizes in the quiet sections; this is a fourth, in the heavy ones).
The brass is the engine's physical model of lips on a tube, the first wind instrument on the record.

When all four guitars pick the small riff again at 3:32, the kick goes the other way. Run the rule backwards once: a long of three sixteenths is a long of two and a short of one, a short of two is one long. So the foot stops doubling 'stroke, stroke, rest' and plays 'stroke, rest, stroke'; under each held chord it adds a pickup. After 21 sixteenths (3:36) the bass and the two inside guitars go with it: in each muted long cell the wall pair strikes twice and the low end answers in the gap. note: v13, FOUR KETTLEDRUMS (palette: the kick's soft strokes in the middle quiet section go to tuned drums; a new song-local patch, `em-kettle`, the record's first use of the engine's kettledrum modes). LISTEN FOR 2:38–3:05, and the last second and a half before the band at 3:05. One size of cell had no tune anywhere: 13 and 8 sixteenths. Under the band those cells are the chord; in the quiet sections they were only the foot, thirteen soft kicks. In the middle quiet section those thirteen strokes are now four kettledrums playing the harp's tune at that size, an octave under the lower harp: A♭, then C♭ and E♭, and on the last cell the one G♭. That last note is rolled, and while it rolls the pedal lets the head down a semitone, so the roll arrives on F with the band: the clean E and B go up to F and C there (v10), and the drum comes down to meet them. The first and third quiet sections keep their foot. WHAT I MEASURED: a stroke sings its written note (the kettle pulls the head's modes to 1 : 1.5 : 2); over the section the drums sit 3.6 dB under the two harps and level with the bowl, each stroke 1.8 to 4.6 dB under everything else together. The roll murmurs at the level of the rest, then for its last 0.4 s stands 5 to 6 dB over it; alone, its pitch holds G♭ until 0.56 s before the band and reads F on arrival. THE COST: the section is 0.46 LU louder (4.4 dB under the band before it; it was 4.9). Every other section, and all five excerpts on the three open cards, moved 0.03 dB or less (the file's loudness trim). Full renders 99.767 → 99.771 and 99.826 → 99.833 (seeds 0, 11), −10.1 LUFS. WHAT THE BENCH TAUGHT (in sounds.md): a roll's strokes must fall a whole, even number of the head's cycles apart or they cancel (strokes every 75 ms left a hole 14 dB deep); `bright` does nothing to a kettle; an expr_path runs to the release, so the patch needs gate=1. WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether soft kettledrums under two harps and a bowl sound like an orchestra pit or like a film score; whether the roll helps the return or crowds the guitar's swelling A♭. Not heard by me. note: SECTION w1, THE TWO LETTERS ON TWO SIDES. LISTEN FOR 0:00–0:10.3, the song’s first cell of 55 sixteenths (flagged static; the stretch the last two notes called unworked). The riff is a word in two letters, long and short, and until now both guitars said every stroke of it together. Here they spell it apart: the chords and the ringing strings are still both guitars, but between them the clipped strokes inside long cells are the left guitar’s alone and the ones inside short cells the right’s. Thirteen strokes left, eight right: the ratio in the title. Bass and foot stay in the middle on every stroke. At 0:10.3, on the first G♭ chord, the two play as one again, and the log drum (on the right) takes the short cells the right guitar has just been saying alone. By subtraction only: 21 strokes are each played by one guitar where two played them (gl gives up 8, gr 13); no note is added or moved, and nothing else in the song changes.
